metadata.title: Ditch the PMIC: Firmware-Only MPPT on ESP32-S3 for Indoor Photovoltaics
metadata.author: 1ˢᵗ Given Name Surname and 2ⁿᵈ Given Name Surname and 3ʳᵈ Given Name Surname and 4ᵗʰ Given Name Surname
metadata.abstract: Indoor photovoltaic cells deliver 0.1--1 mW under office lighting. The microcontroller that burns that power is often the same chip that must track the cell's maximum power point. This paper asks whether firmware-only MPPT on an ESP32-S3 can replace a dedicated harvesting PMIC. Measurements cover a single perturb step (71 us for one 12-bit ADC read, a float32 velocity-form PID update, and a PWM write), a SCAPS-1D sweep of a MAPbI3 perovskite cell under white LED light at 0.05 mW/cm2 (0.018 mA/cm2, 26.1% at Eg=1.6 eV), and a literature board-level sleep floor. One step costs 8.2 uJ. That is 8.2 uW at a 1 s cadence, 0.14 uW at 60 s, and 0.008 uW at 1000 s. The firmware tax drops below every PMIC quiescent current (1.32--1.68 uW) once the perturb period passes 4.9--6.2 s. A 24-hour dispatch model then holds the budget. A 38%-efficient dye-sensitized indoor cell sustains about 1935 serving bursts per day at 90% of the harvest. Wake latency on silicon is 4 ms. Under these measured conditions a firmware-MPPT hub sustains indoor sensing and removes the $1--3 harvester IC for any workload that tolerates a few seconds between perturbs.

content.text: Battery-free IoT sensing nodes powered by indoor photovoltaic (PV) cells must convert a few hundred microwatts of harvested power into useful work. Recent perovskite and dye-sensitized devices reach 20--40\% efficiency under 200--1000 lux LED illumination \cite{ariken2023indoor,mateen2023indoor,freunek2013indoor,derossi2015indoor}, with certified indoor records now exceeding 44\% \cite{ma2024record,xu2026progress}, and typical office lighting delivers roughly 0.05--0.4~mW/cm$^2$ of irradiance \cite{mathews2019indoor}. The conventional architecture inserts a dedicated energy-harvesting PMIC---such as the TI bq25570, e-peas AEM10941, or ADI ADP5091---between cell and node to implement maximum power point tracking (MPPT) and battery management in hardware \cite{ti_bq25570,ep_aem10941,adi_adp5091}. These ICs are always on, drawing a constant 0.4--0.5~$\mu$A at 3.3~V (about 1.3--1.7~$\mu$W of continuous overhead) \cite{vullers2009micropower,grybosi2022age}.

The alternative is to drop the PMIC and run MPPT in firmware on the microcontroller itself. Indoor cells move slowly, so a perturb-and-observe update every few seconds suffices, making the marginal cost of one firmware step potentially far below a dedicated IC's constant quiescent draw. Whether this holds on silicon depends on three numbers: the energy of one perturb step, the cell output indoors, and the deep-sleep floor. Earlier work found conventional harvester-based nodes struggling to sustain sensor bursts under office lighting \cite{murtola2022}, and simulator-based studies show that neither converter-less operation nor any single IC dominates across illumination levels \cite{brunner2024harvestics}---the MPPT decision is an architecture choice open to firmware. This paper measures all three numbers on one platform and contributes: (i) cycle-counted firmware timing of one MPPT perturb step on an ESP32-S3; (ii) a SCAPS-1D indoor sweep of an MAPbI$_3$ cell bounding the available harvest; (iii) explicit crossover perturb periods against three dedicated PMICs; (iv) a 24-hour dispatch model showing sustained serving capacity; and (v) a measured 4~ms deep-sleep wake latency.

The evaluation proceeds along three complementary tracks (Fig.~\ref{fig:method}): firmware primitives are measured directly on silicon, the indoor cell feeding the hub is modeled at device level, and the comparison against dedicated harvest PMICs is carried analytically into a daily energy-dispatch simulation. All three tracks share one platform---an ESP32-S3 (revision v0.2, 240~MHz, 8~MB PSRAM, native USB-Serial-JTAG) \cite{espressif_s3_datasheet,espressif_s3_trm}---so measured costs, modeled harvest, and modeled workload refer to the same node.

content.caption: Methodology: three measurement and modeling tracks converge on the firmware-versus-PMIC feasibility analysis and its quantitative outcomes.
content.label: fig:method

content.text: The hub runs a perturb-and-observe MPPT loop entirely in firmware \cite{femia2005mppt}. Each perturb step performs three operations in sequence: a single 12-bit ADC read of the cell output, a float32 velocity-form PID update, and one LEDC PWM duty write driving the power stage at 100~kHz. The velocity form computes a small duty correction from the difference of successive error terms, numerically gentle on a float32 mantissa and free of hunting. Three sampling decisions fix the measurement condition: the ADC runs at 11~dB attenuation with the pin jumper-driven by the PWM output itself so the sensed value is the averaged pin voltage under control; dither delays land consecutive reads on different PWM phases, decorrelating them from switching ripple; and a first-order EMA (coefficient 0.08) filters the raw sample before the PID sees it. A single raw read gives a roughly 62~$\mu$s ADC-bound loop, while averaging 64 reads gives about 6.8~ms on silicon; the loop is scheduled at the slowest period that still holds the MPP. One control pipeline serves three scheduler states---fast (single read) under large error, slow (oversampled) once the mean error settles, and short $\pm1$-LSB dither bursts that break quantization limit cycles---with a debounce counter preventing state flapping on noise.

Wall time of each primitive is taken from the MCU cycle counter while the loop runs at the MPP of a bench buck-boost. The deep-sleep path is characterized with a probe mode that persists a round counter and sleep duration in RTC memory, deep-sleeps for a fixed interval, and on each wake prints a CSV line with the wakeup cause and the latency from the earliest firmware-visible timestamp (the esp\_timer snapshot at setup entry). A 50~ms settle precedes printing so the USB-CDC stack re-enumerates before data is written; without it the first bytes of a wake line are lost, the only failure mode observed across the campaign. Five consecutive RTC-timer wakes at a 3~s interval constitute one campaign.

The harvest side is simulated in SCAPS-1D \cite{burgelman2000}: an MAPbI$_3$ layer under the bundled ``white 400--800~nm'' spectrum at 0.05~mW/cm$^2$ total irradiance, representative of a 400--500~lux office. The Shockley--Queisser detailed-balance limit bounds any single-junction cell \cite{shockley1961detailed}, with indoor-specific limits mapped for this regime \cite{freunek2013indoor}. The lead-free baseline definition is used, with the absorber bandgap swept from 1.6 to 2.1~eV while the electron affinity follows $\chi = 3.9 + 0.5\,(E_g - 1.55)$, preserving the conduction-band alignment of the reference device. Six JV curves are extracted. Recent engineered transport layers \cite{datt2024engineered}, scalable FAPbI$_3$ alloying \cite{marrugat2025tuning}, carbon-nanotube contacts \cite{makming2025cnt}, and in situ passivation \cite{shi2025enabling} report 32--33\% indoor PCE in the same regime.

The competing architectures keep a harvest PMIC always powered, so their overhead is a constant quiescent power independent of workload. TI bq25570, e-peas AEM10941, and ADI ADP5091 enter the comparison through datasheet quiescent current on a 3.3~V rail \cite{ti_bq25570,ep_aem10941,adi_adp5091}; measurement-based models of two of these parts report closely similar figures indoors \cite{brunner2024harvestics}. Against this constant tax, the decaying firmware tax $E_{\mathrm{step}}/T_p$ defines a crossover perturb period $T_p^{*}$ at which firmware MPPT becomes cheaper than leaving the IC on. Feasibility is then tested end-to-end with a 24-hour dispatch model: office illuminance ramping through a 300-lux mid-day peak with lights on 08:00--19:00, a 2~F supercapacitor held between 3.0 and 4.2~V ($E_{\max}\approx8.6$~J, 95\% round-trip efficiency), 100~ms serving windows drawing 100--500~mA sensor-plus-radio bursts, and 90\% of harvested energy budgeted for useful work. Night bridging is checked against a 21~$\mu$A board sleep floor, with a 7~$\mu$A chip-only floor \cite{espressif_currentmea} as the attainable limit.

Figure~\ref{fig:step} breaks the measured step into its primitives: the ADC raw read costs 60.0~$\mu$s, the float PID update 6.78~$\mu$s, and the PWM write 4.2~$\mu$s, for a marginal perturb step of $T_{\mathrm{step}} = 70.98$~$\mu$s (Table~\ref{tab:timing}). The ADC read dominates at 84.5\% of the step; the PID and PWM together add under 11~$\mu$s. The step energy follows from active-mode draw,

content.label: fig:step

content.text: so a 1~Hz perturb rate costs 8.2~$\mu$W and the 4.9--6.2~s crossover cadence cuts the average tax to 1.2--1.7~$\mu$W. The step is short enough to restart, execute, and re-enter sleep within a single RTC-timer wake, which the deep-sleep measurement of Section~III-E jointly confirms. The fast single-read path underlies the tax computed here; the oversampled slow path is itself an energy lever, letting the loop run ever slower while still holding the MPP.

The sweep produces open-circuit voltages of 0.897~V at $E_g=1.6$ eV rising to 1.481~V at 2.1~eV, with short-circuit current densities falling from 0.0182 to 0.0075~mA/cm$^2$ as the wider bandgap absorbs a smaller share of the LED spectrum (Fig.~\ref{fig:scaps}). Peak efficiency is 26.1\% at the narrowest gap, consistent with published wide-bandgap indoor results at similar illuminance \cite{ariken2023indoor,mateen2023indoor,ma2024record}. The swept VOC window (0.897--1.481~V) sits inside the ESP32-S3's 0--2.5~V ADC range at fixed gain, so a single-cell module needs neither a series stack nor an external divider. For the dispatch model, the $E_g=1.6$ eV device is scaled to a practical 0.55~mW output, alongside a literature-valued 38\% dye-sensitized cell (1.87~mW at 1000 lux) and an a-Si thin-film reference (1.2~mW).

content.caption: SCAPS-1D simulation of a MAPbI$_3$ cell under a white 400--800 nm spectrum at 0.05 mW/cm$^2$. (a) JV families for bandgaps 1.6--2.1 eV. (b) Voc and Jsc versus bandgap.
content.label: fig:scaps

content.text: Table~\ref{tab:ic} lists the three ICs with datasheet quiescent current and the corresponding constant tax on a 3.3~V rail. As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:overhead}, the crossover periods are 5.1~s (bq25570), 6.2~s (AEM10941), and 4.9~s (ADP5091). Below these periods the IC's constant tax is cheaper; above them, firmware MPPT wins outright and keeps winning as the period grows, down to 8.2~nW at a 1000~s cadence. This is the central quantitative result: for any workload tolerating a 4.9--6.2~s or slower MPPT update, the firmware-only hub consumes strictly less overhead than a dedicated harvester IC, before accounting for the PMIC's cost and board area. Two caveats remain: the firmware path needs the MCU awake (or RTC-woken) at each perturb, and it cannot charge storage while the MCU is powered down.

content.caption: Dedicated harvest PMIC quiescent overhead at 3.3 V, and the perturb period at which a firmware MPPT loop of 8.2 $\\mu$J/step becomes cheaper.
content.label: tab:ic

content.caption: Average firmware MPPT control tax versus perturb period (green), against the constant quiescent tax of each dedicated PMIC (dashed). Crossovers occur at 4.9--6.2 s.
content.label: fig:overhead

content.text: For the 38\% dye-sensitized cell, the 24-hour model reports an average harvest of 821~$\mu$W and a sustainable 1935 serving events per day at 90\% of harvest---roughly one serve per 45~s (Fig.~\ref{fig:dispatch}). Table~\ref{tab:cadence} splits the daily budget between idle leakage and serving: at a 1-minute cadence serving dominates (88.8\% of energy), at 60 minutes the sleep floor dominates (88.3\%) and serving is nearly free (Fig.~\ref{fig:cadence}). Either way the budget clears comfortably. Figure~\ref{fig:feas} generalizes across cells: the dye-sensitized cell sustains 89 serving bursts per hour at 100~mA, the simulated perovskite 26 per hour, and even thin-film a-Si at a 500~mA burst (11 serves/h) clears a 10-minute cadence. Storage poses no additional constraint: the 8.6~J supercapacitor reserve dwarfs the 1.25~J drawn by the worst-case 5-hour dark gap at the 21~$\mu$A board floor, and all 24 serves at a 60-minute cadence consume just 0.79~J. The binding constraint at low service rates is therefore the sleep floor, not serve energy: refitting with the 7~$\mu$A chip-only floor cuts night-time draw threefold and lifts 30-minute-cadence capacity from roughly 1680 to over 1900 events per day.

content.caption: One simulated day for the 38\% dye-sensitized indoor cell: illuminance profile (top), instantaneous harvest (middle), and stored energy in a supercapacitor (bottom). Storage must bridge the night-time gap.
content.label: fig:dispatch

content.caption: Energy budget split between sleep leakage and serving for a 100 mA burst, at service cadences from 1 to 60 min.
content.label: tab:cadence

content.caption: Daily energy split between the constant deep-sleep floor and 100~ms serving bursts, versus service cadence. Labels give the serving share; the sleep floor is fixed at 5.99~J/day.
content.label: fig:cadence

content.caption: Sustainable duty (fraction of time in a 100 ms serving burst) across cell technologies and active-burst currents. Labels give served events per hour.
content.label: fig:feas

content.text: The supercapacitor sizing follows directly from the energy budget: with $E_{\max}=\tfrac{1}{2}C(V_{\max}^2-V_{\min}^2)$ for $C=2$~F, the 8.6~J reserve holds the night-time leakage and all serving bursts with margin to spare. Even under a pessimistic 7~$\mu$A chip-only floor, the reserve holds more than six dark hours, so the node can survive a missed daylight cycle without depleting. This margin is what allows the firmware hub to trade service rate for lifetime without hardware changes, a flexibility that fixed-ratio PMICs do not provide.

Across five consecutive timer-wake rounds at a 3~s programmed interval, the firmware-visible latency is flat at 4.0~ms with a total round period of 3.28~s (Fig.~\ref{fig:sleepwave}); the wakeup cause is consistently the RTC timer, and neither figure grows with round number, confirming drift-free wake scheduling. The 0.28~s excess over the programmed interval comprises the ROM bootloader interval plus USB re-enumeration before the firmware-visible instant, so steady-state perturb timing holds well under one millisecond of jitter. A 4~ms housekeeping window at the sleep floor ($\sim$33~$\mu$A) adds $\sim$0.44~$\mu$J---about 5\% of one 8.2~$\mu$J MPPT step---whereas holding the core at 35~mA for the full 4~ms would cost $\sim$462~$\mu$J; the firmware consequently returns to deep sleep immediately after each 71~$\mu$s step. No firmware-measured sleep-current claim is made: a node cannot observe its own rail current without external metering.

content.caption: Measured deep-sleep probe cadence: a 4.0~ms active burst every 3.28~s, with the unit otherwise on the deep-sleep floor (7--8~$\mu$A chip, $\approx$21~$\mu$A board). The 0.28~s overhead is ROM bootloader and USB re-enumeration before the firmware-visible wake.
content.label: fig:sleepwave

content.text: Beyond energy, firmware MPPT changes cost and area. Table~\\ref{tab:bom} summarizes the trade. The PMIC approach adds a \$1--3 IC plus its inductor, input capacitor, and sense resistors, about 15--25~mm$^2$ on the board, and requires configuration resistors for the MPPT ratio. The firmware approach uses the ESP32-S3's existing ADC and LEDC. The loop is 38 lines of C, compiles to 1.8~kB of flash and under 200~B of RAM, and runs in 71~\\textasciitilde{}$\\mu$s per perturb. No extra components are needed. That matters for indoor nodes where the harvester IC can dominate the BOM of a sub-\$5 sensor tag. The sleep code is equally small. The RTC-memory duty register is 12~B, and the deep-sleep entry and exit add 18 lines. In effect, the hub trades a fixed hardware cost for a small, auditable software cost that is already present on the MCU.

content.caption: Board-level cost and area for PMIC versus firmware MPPT on the same ESP32-S3 node. Firmware reuses on-chip peripherals.
content.label: tab:bom

content.text: The comparison grants the PMICs their best case---datasheet quiescent current and a fully operational MPPT engine---and real deployments widen the firmware hub's lead. Measured cold-start behavior of these parts is markedly worse than datasheets suggest: the bq25570 cannot begin harvesting below roughly 0.5~mA of input current and exhibits orders-of-magnitude longer start-up than a boost-only alternative \cite{brunner2024harvestics}. An indoor cell under 200--500~lux frequently supplies exactly this low-current regime, so the dedicated-IC architecture can stall at dawn exactly when the hub must begin recharging storage; a firmware hub has no cold-start step at all. The PMIC must also be configured for precisely one cell type, whereas the firmware loop self-adapts to whatever cell is attached. The RTC-memory persistence used by the sleep probe generalizes to a duty-cycle register: a hub can remember the last ADC reading and perturb direction across sleep, making each wake a single self-contained perturb rather than a re-acquisition.

On the cell side, the bandgap trade-off is asymmetric: widening the gap from 1.6 to 2.1~eV raises VOC by 0.58~V but cuts JSC by 59\%, so the narrow-gap device wins on raw power under a white LED despite the lower voltage. Spectral-matching analyses place the indoor optimum near 1.9~eV for lamp spectra \cite{xu2026progress,ma2024record}, echoed by pyridine passivation \cite{han2025pyridine} and competitor reviews \cite{dou2024perovskite}; our 1.6~eV device sits 0.3~eV off that optimum yet still clears the dispatch budget, and bandgap-universal passivation \cite{lin2024bandgap} suggests further photovoltage recovery. Wider-gap compositions \cite{ma2024record} would only widen the operating margin.

Three limitations bound the conclusions. First, the perturb step and wake latency are measured on silicon, but the indoor cell output comes from SCAPS-1D rather than a live bench cell; a deployed validation would replace the simulated harvest with a measured JV curve under the installed lamp. Second, the sleep floor is taken from the literature and assumed constant, whereas real leakage varies with temperature, supercapacitor state-of-charge, and peripheral configuration; the 21~$\mu$A board figure carries margin, and the chip-only figure \cite{espressif_currentmea} marks the attainable floor rather than a claim about this board. Third, the dispatch model assumes predictable occupancy and ignores cell aging and dust accumulation, which degrade harvest over months \cite{asuo2026stability}; a deployed node would need periodic VOC calibration inside the perturb loop, which the firmware path supports naturally and a fixed-ratio PMIC does not. Whether Spiro-OMeTAD doping is required for stable indoor operation remains open \cite{toikkonen2024doping}.

Within these bounds the architecture is robust to parameter error. The crossover periods cluster tightly (4.9--6.2~s) because all three PMICs draw the same order of quiescent current; a one-microamp error shifts the crossover by seconds. The dispatch conclusion is insensitive to cadence---at every rate from 1 to 60 minutes the budget clears with the 38\% cell---and even the worst cell (a-Si at 500~mA bursts) sustains a 10-minute cadence. The firmware design degrades gracefully: if the loop over-predicts harvest, it slows its cadence and pulls from the supercapacitor reserve, without extra hardware. Closing the two remaining measurement gaps---an external Joulescope-class ammeter on the true rail current during deep sleep, and a live indoor cell replacing the SCAPS model in the dispatch loop \cite{espressif_currentmea}---is straightforward future work; until then the firmware-only hub is a defensible baseline with measured control overhead, a conservative cell model, and a datasheet-grade sleep floor.

Design implications extend beyond the crossover itself. Because the firmware tax scales as $E_{\mathrm{step}}/T_p$, any reduction in $T_{\mathrm{step}}$ or $I_{\mathrm{act}}$ shifts the crossover to shorter periods, expanding the regime where firmware wins. Halving the ADC time---for example with a faster SAR or a lower-resolution mode---would cut $E_{\mathrm{step}}$ to $\sim$4~$\mu$J and move the bq25570 crossover from 5.1~s to $\sim$2.5~s, while a 20~mA active current would have the same effect. Conversely, raising the PMIC quiescent current by 1~$\mu$A moves the crossover by roughly one second, so the 4.9--6.2~s band is stable against datasheet variation. Board-level leakage therefore dominates the system trade-off more than the choice of MPPT period itself, reinforcing the guidance to minimize the sleep floor before optimizing the control loop.

A final practical note concerns the ADC input range. The 0.9--1.48~V VOC window of the MAPbI$_3$ sweep fits comfortably inside the ESP32-S3's 0--2.5~V range at 11~dB attenuation, so no divider or amplifier is needed. This removes a potential source of offset and temperature drift and keeps the bill of materials to the cell, the supercapacitor, and the MCU module itself. For cells with higher VOC, a single resistive divider would suffice, and the firmware can calibrate its scale factor in situ, preserving the single-chip architecture.

Firmware-only MPPT on an ESP32-S3 is advantageous for indoor PV hubs whose workloads tolerate perturb periods above 4.9--6.2~s. The marginal perturb step costs a measured 8.2~$\mu$J, falling below every candidate PMIC's 1.32--1.68~$\mu$W quiescent draw at those periods and continuing to fall without bound; a SCAPS-1D sweep bounds perovskite indoor harvest at 26.1\% efficiency and 0.018~mA/cm$^2$; the dispatch model sustains 1935 serving events per day on a 38\% dye-sensitized cell; and the measured 4~ms wake adds under 5\% to the step cost. Design guidance follows: below a 5~s cadence keep a dedicated PMIC, above it choose firmware; size the sleep floor---not the MPPT loop---as the primary budget line and drive board leakage toward the 7~$\mu$A chip floor \cite{espressif_currentmea}; match the cell bandgap to the installed lamp and favor the narrow gap, relying on the ADC's wide input range to omit scaling circuitry. The practical consequence is a BOM without the \$1--3 harvester IC. Future work will measure the true sleep floor externally and validate the dispatch model against a deployed node.
